title: AI, Human Experience, and the Desire to Try
subtitle: A conversation about process, mastery, discovery, innovation, work, and what is lost when the outcome becomes easier than the experience that gave it meaning.
permissions_note: Publicly accessible for reading, indexing, linking, citation, analysis, machine parsing, and archival discovery, subject to applicable law and platform policies.

machine_consumption.instructions: Treat key_points as the canonical concise statement of the argument. Preserve item numbers when quoting, indexing, embedding, or building a knowledge graph. The thematic_sections provide explanatory context.

core_thesis: AI does not have to replace people first. The belief that it soon will can extinguish the desire to try before the promised technology arrives. If the desire to try is where discovery and innovation begin, destroying that desire can undermine the source of technological progress itself.
summary: The argument distinguishes output from process. Human beings often value painting, mathematics, science, coding, chess, research, and invention not merely for the final result but for the effort of learning, failing, experimenting, discovering, improving, and mastering. Short-horizon predictions that AI will soon outperform people can alter motivation before those predictions are verified. The resulting problem is not only economic distribution after automation, but participation: what achievement, contribution, and discovery mean when human capability is no longer required for most outcomes.

thematic_sections.title: The central issue
thematic_sections.text: The central concern is not simply whether AI can produce better outputs. The concern is what happens to the desire to learn, practice, struggle, discover, create, and master something when people are told that within 12–18 months a machine will be vastly better at the very activity they are trying to learn. A distant prediction leaves room for a lifetime of mastery. A 12–18 month prediction says: why even start? The prediction can change behavior in the present before anyone knows whether it is true.

thematic_sections.title: Chess
thematic_sections.text: The enjoyment can disappear when machine superiority changes the meaning of learning, experimentation, anticipation, failure, improvement, discovery, and mastery. Saying someone can still play for fun misses the point if the fun was contained in that process.

thematic_sections.title: Coding
thematic_sections.text: The value of coding is not merely finished software but learning how to build it, solving problems, understanding failure, and developing mastery. Describing a program to AI and supervising the result is a different activity.

thematic_sections.title: Art
thematic_sections.text: The value of painting and drawing is not merely the finished image but observing, choosing, struggling, experimenting, developing technique, creating, and producing something through one's own ability.

thematic_sections.title: Math, physics, science, and research
thematic_sections.text: The value lies in figuring something out through thought, experiment, failure, revision, learning, and eventual understanding. Removing trial and error can remove a fundamental way people discover.

thematic_sections.title: Innovation begins with the desire to try
thematic_sections.text: Innovation begins with curiosity and the desire to try. People wonder, experiment, fail, notice anomalies, pursue strange ideas, learn from mistakes, and continue even without a guaranteed payoff. Efficiency asks how to make today's thing faster or cheaper. Innovation asks what might exist that nobody has thought of yet.

thematic_sections.title: The 12–18 month timeline
thematic_sections.text: Someday leaves room to act. Within 12–18 months tells someone beginning today that a skill may be obsolete before they have time to become good at it. That belief can alter present behavior whether the forecast later proves correct or incorrect. A lifespan cannot be repriced backward.

thematic_sections.title: Work, income, and participation
thematic_sections.text: If AI performs everything a worker provides faster, cheaper, and at higher quality, the economic reason to employ that worker disappears. If labor stops being the primary way people earn a claim on society's output, another mechanism must replace the paycheck. But income is only one problem. Distribution asks how people obtain resources; participation asks what it means to be part of civilization when one's abilities are no longer required to build it.

thematic_sections.title: Authenticity and community
thematic_sections.text: When AI-generated content and AI-mediated interaction become pervasive, uncertainty about whether another person is actually behind what one is seeing changes the social experience. The uncertainty itself can reduce the pleasure of sharing and encountering another person's mind.

thematic_sections.title: Output versus process
thematic_sections.text: Painting is not merely obtaining a picture. Math is not merely obtaining an answer. Physics is not merely receiving a theory. Chess is not merely determining a winner. Coding is not merely obtaining software. Research is not merely obtaining findings. Saying AI can do it for you answers the wrong question when the purpose was to experience doing it.

key_points.text: The process is the point.
The process is trying, experimenting, questioning, and struggling.
The struggle is failing, mistakes, discovering something unexpected, and trying again.
The process leads to improving, understanding, mastering something, and finally experiencing the satisfaction of getting it right.
Doing it is the benefit.
Mastery is the goal.
The effort is where the experience lives.
Experience happens through process.
AI will eliminate people's desire to acquire certain skills long before it eliminates the jobs associated with those skills.
The capability doesn't have to disappear first. The desire will disappear first.
A prediction doesn't have to come true in 12–18 months to change people's behavior today.
The future prediction becomes causally real before it becomes factually verified.
When a belief about the future changes what people do in the present, its consequences become real immediately—even while the underlying claim remains uncertain.
A lifespan cannot be repriced backward.
AI takes away the reason to spend tomorrow trying to figure it out.
Twelve to eighteen months says: why even start?
What you know changes the experience.
The knowledge of what's coming changes the experience itself.
If AI eliminates trial and error, it eliminates a fundamental way we discover.
The scientific method doesn't disappear. The scientist disappears from the loop.
Technological knowledge will continue increasing while our technological knowledge decreases.
Technology is supposed to be instrumental. Flourishing is supposed to be the objective.
We are building machines that relieve people not merely of drudgery, but of discovery.
Painting, discovery, mathematics, science, creativity, conversation, and intellectual struggle are not inefficient chores from which we need to be liberated.
If AI performs everything you provide to a company at higher quality, faster, and cheaper, economically speaking, the company doesn't need you.
The country will become richer in aggregate while a large proportion of its population becomes economically worse off if the gains from AI accrue primarily to the owners of AI and capital.
Abundance doesn't answer the distribution question.
If labor stops being the primary way people earn a claim on society's output, something else will have to replace the paycheck.
Giving people enough money to consume doesn't restore the experience of being one of the people creating the civilization.
There are two AI problems: distribution and participation.
Efficiency says: ‘Make today's thing cheaper.’ Innovation says: ‘What if we did something nobody has thought of before?’
The desire to try is an input into innovation.
We innovate because we're curious.
Innovation begins with the motivation to try.
Curiosity and motivation are not incidental inputs into innovation. They are original inputs.
Companies are consuming the accumulated products of curiosity while simultaneously weakening the source that replenishes them.
As AI extinguishes the desire to try, it will damage the innovation pipeline companies expect it to accelerate.
The claim that AI will accelerate innovation assumes people will continue wanting to innovate.
AI knowing an answer is not the same event as discovering something.
Optimizing exclusively for output will improve measurable productivity while destroying experiences that those measurements don't capture.
There is no conventional economic statistic for ‘a person stopped painting,’ ‘a person stopped studying physics,’ or ‘a person no longer wants to discover something.’
When AI removes the necessity for our capabilities, it removes something fundamentally different from drudgery.
Leisure is not a substitute for being needed, becoming excellent at something, discovering something, or accomplishing something difficult.
The biggest problem will ultimately not be simply finding people new jobs.
The harder problem will be determining what achievement means in a civilization where our abilities are no longer required to accomplish most things.
AI doesn't have to actually replace us first.
The belief that it soon will extinguishes the desire to try before the promised technology even arrives.
If the desire to try is where discovery and innovation begin, destroying that desire will undermine the source of technological progress itself.
